speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It will replace the Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act 1980 (PHMCA), which was enacted in 1980 and regulates the use of premises in which healthcare services are provided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This phased approach is intended to give licensees sufficient time to prepare for, and adjust to, the new Act, and thus minimise disruption to existing healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Since the implementation of HCSA in Phase 1, there have been developments which require further refinement of this legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, the COVID-19 pandemic has led to changes in how healthcare is delivered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For instance, new models of care such as teleconsulting and home medical services have proven to be effective and efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While HCSA is already a services-based framework, it needs to provide more clarity and flexibility on the requirements related to these new models of care, to continue protecting patient safety and enabling new innovations in providing care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: COVID-19 also highlighted the need for HCSA to be adjusted to allow us to respond to public healthcare emergencies more nimbly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This includes instances where licence conditions must be changed immediately to address urgent patient safety or public health issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Second, we received feedback on several areas of the regulatory framework, which could be improved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This includes misleading advertisements including non-licensable healthcare services or business names.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This was a result of engagements with stakeholders to continuously review and update HCSA while preparing for its rollout across existing and new licensees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: And third, there was a need to align the scope of regulatory action for healthcare advertising by licensees and non-licensees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: All these have led us to further review HCSA to enhance and future-proof the legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The proposed amendments will allow us to be nimbler in responding to the evolving healthcare landscape and enable premises-neutral care to be delivered across our healthcare settings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It will also strengthen governance to safeguard patient safety and welfare, and protect patients from misinformation, exploitation or abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 4 will amend section 9 to introduce the regulation of four primary modes of service delivery: permanent premises, temporary premises, conveyances and remote provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Licensees must obtain approval to provide a licensable healthcare service by any of these four modes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To give some examples, permanent premises are physical, in-person, General practitioner clinics or hospitals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Temporary premises would include ad-hoc health screenings in a community centre's multipurpose hall or when a doctor conducts a house call visit to a patient's home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Conveyances refer to the healthcare service being delivered using vehicles, like ambulances or dental screening buses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Remote provision involves the delivery of healthcare services through virtual platforms such as virtual teleconsultation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: A clear regulatory framework for these various service delivery modes will give providers the confidence to continue to provide and expand home care services, which are critical to enable ageing in the community, in particular for seniors who are homebound, or those at the end-of-life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Bringing medical services closer to the community and into homes will also enhance the convenience to patients and their caregivers and reduce caregiver burden.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, home medical providers caring for patients at the end-of-life will now be able to help maximise patients' quality of life and fulfil their aspirations to spend their last days at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Mobile Inpatient Care at Home (MIC@Home) is another care model where suitable patients can choose to be managed at home and receive similar clinical care as in the hospital, and this includes regular review by the care team either by home visits, teleconsultation or remote monitoring of vital signs, and even intravenous medication if required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under this approval regime, the Ministry of Health (MOH) can prescribe regulatory requirements and impose approval conditions on licensees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MOH can also prescribe the service delivery modes that are not permitted for a licensable healthcare service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This provides licensees with better clarity on the requirements they must meet and allows them to determine the appropriate business model for the delivery of their healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This also increases public transparency on the nature of healthcare services being provided by each licensee, how they can access these services and how the Ministry intends to regulate the delivery of the various types of healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The amendments at clauses 6 to 9, and 12 to 15, in particular the new sections 9, 11A and 11B and the amended section 20, set out the details of the approval regime for this, including the regulatory actions that can be taken against licensees who contravene the relevant regulatory requirements or approval conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: At present, MOH issues licence conditions to impose new safety standards, such as in instances where there is a change in the regulatory technical standards due to evolving scientific developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MOH is now required to provide licensees with a minimum period of 14 days to send in written representation in response to the intent to amend the licence conditions, if any.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is so that MOH can expeditiously implement new healthcare protocols to protect public health and patient safety under exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To further safeguard patient safety and welfare upfront, two other approval regimes will be introduced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, for Specified Services which involve more complex or higher risk procedures provided in a licensable healthcare service, and therefore have distinct requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Examples of Specified Services are liposuction, endoscopy, or radiation oncology services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Having an approval process enables MOH to better verify that all requisite standards are met before a licensee can provide such a service, so that patient safety and welfare are upheld before these services are delivered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This approval regime builds on the approval process that is currently available for special care services in medical clinics and specialised procedures and services in private hospitals under the PHMCA framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Second, for the appointment of a Clinical Governance Officer or CGO.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under HCSA, a CGO is expected to play a crucial role in overseeing the clinical governance and technical aspects of healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: By requiring licensees to seek approval for the appointment of a CGO, MOH can also ensure upfront that a competent and suitable individual is appointed and better safeguard patient safety and welfare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Besides enhancing upfront safeguards, clause 18 also re-enacts section 28 to introduce flexibility for MOH to vary the scope of restrictions for selected individuals or groups of individuals employed or engaged in different healthcare settings, based on the anticipated risk of patient harm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under the current HCSA, certain licensees may be prohibited from employing any individual who has committed egregious crimes involving violent acts such as rape or kidnapping, except with the approval from MOH, regardless of the duties performed by the individual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is done to protect the safety and well-being of more vulnerable patients, as they may not be able to fend for themselves if they are harmed or abused.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is similar to the approach taken under the Early Childhood Development Centres Act 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: However, the risk of patient harm varies depending on the role undertaken or performed by these personnel and the nature of the healthcare settings they work in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Hence, clause 18 will repeal and re-enact section 28 to provide some flexibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The restrictions will apply to prospective employees and those engaged, but not employed, by licensees to undertake work in healthcare settings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For a start, licensees operating in the Institute of Mental Health  and all nursing homes and hospices will be required to comply with these restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is because there have been a number of cases of physical violence or abuse reported at these types of healthcare institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MOH will continue to monitor for any emerging trends that indicate an increased risk of patient harm in other settings and will consider extending these restrictions to other individuals or settings in the future if needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The proposed amendments also seek to enable the public to make better informed choices about their use of healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In particular, the necessity of ensuring that consumers or patients are not misinformed or unduly influenced to inappropriately consume certain healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are addressing this with tighter controls on advertising and naming.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To clarify, the specialist must be locally registered to practise the specialty in question, and can either be employed or engaged by the licensee to provide the approved licensable healthcare service under the auspices of the licensee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Specialties recognised under the Medical Registration Act or the Dental Registration Act and their associated terms are the specialty names intended to be covered by the amended section 29.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, a clinic cannot be called "The Neurology Clinic" or the "The Brain Clinic" if there is no neurologist practising in that clinic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This protects patients from being misled into thinking they are receiving specialty care where the provider is not a specialist.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Licensees are currently prohibited under HCSA from using the terms "Singapore" or "National" in their names or logos except with the approval of the Director of Medical Services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To further prevent public misperceptions, the prohibition against using these terms under section 29 will be amended to extend to the same terms in any language, not just English.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To clarify, existing licensees will be allowed to retain their current business names if it contains the terms "Singapore" or "National", unless there are changes in the business name or licensee in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These requirements include the prohibition on non-HCSA licensees who claim in healthcare service advertising to "treat" any medical conditions or diseases under the new section 31A inserted by Clause 22.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, non-HCSA licensees cannot claim that "We treat chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes and all cardiac conditions" or that "We are experienced in treating scoliosis".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: At present, there is a disparity in enforcement actions between the two Acts, with MASA having significantly lower penalties and a more limited scope of regulatory action, for example, there is no power to take down non-compliant advertisements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The new section 31C inserted by Clause 22 will impose similar penalties for comparable non-compliance in healthcare service advertising regardless of whether one is an errant provider of a non-licensable healthcare service, or a HCSA licensee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This will deter non-HCSA licensees and ensure all healthcare service providers are held to the same high standards when advertising their healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Lastly, many stakeholders have also raised concerns about cases of misuse of the title "Doctor" in healthcare service advertising by certain non-registered healthcare professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These restrictions will not apply to registered healthcare professionals such as nurses and pharmacists, as they are regulated under their respective Professional Acts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Non-registered healthcare practitioners who are PhD holders and wish to use the title "Doctor" in advertisements of healthcare services must also state their qualification and a disclaimer that the qualification is not a medical or dental qualification, in such advertisements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: However, for settings beyond healthcare service advertising, for example, the use of "Doctor" by PhD holders in academic articles, this requirement will not apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We understand that there are instances of foreign-trained doctors or dentists who have proper medical or dental qualifications, but do not have these qualifications registered with the Singapore Medical Council (SMC) or Singapore Dental Council (SDC).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There are also instances of doctors and dentists who have previously registered themselves locally but have allowed the registration to lapse as they are now retired.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In both these cases, should these practitioners wish to use the title "Doctor" in healthcare service advertising, the amended Act will require them to additionally include a disclaimer that they do not hold a valid practicing certificate issued by the SMC or SDC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As these doctors and dentists are not locally registered, these incremental restrictions are designed to ensure that they are treated similarly as other non-registered healthcare professionals, for parity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The amendments at clauses 25 and 28 pertain to the redesignation of the "Director of Medical Services" to the "Director-General of Health".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This new designation is a more accurate reflection of the job scope and responsibilities of the Director of Medical Services, which goes beyond medical services to also the control of communicable and non-communicable diseases, the setting of healthcare professional standards and development and enhancing performance of the healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, the redesignation of the Director of Medical Services will be implemented within two months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOH's report of the public consultation shows that the feedback was constructive and that the Bill we see today contains changes made due to the public consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOH will continue this good practice of consulting the public before making changes to the law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first area for clarification is on the regulation of telemedicine.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill will require entities providing telemedicine services to be licensed and regulated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will MOH regulate the risks posed by telemedicine?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOH has also facilitated it through its Licensing Experiment and Adaptation Programme as well as the Voluntary Listing of Direct Telemedicine Service Providers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Certain risks and concerns may be more prominent in telemedicine than in conventional medicine.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of in-person and physical examination may be more likely to prompt instances and claims of misdiagnosis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The online nature of doctor-patient interactions and the relative ease of recording these interactions may also increase the risk of breaches in doctor-patient confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is not to mention the role of hackers, fraudsters, phishers and other cybersecurity threats that may see value in gaining access to the vulnerable and personal moments of doctor-patient consultations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister provide details and examples on how it will leverage this licensing regime to regulate telemedicine?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will these regulations compel changes to ethical and professional codes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the removal of the 14-day notice requirement for modifications of a licence condition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An example provided by MOH of a situation that may require quick changes to licensing conditions is COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The stakeholder consultations on the amendments raised concerns about frequent updates in healthcare protocols that are understandably disruptive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To help licensees better understand the exceptional situations where licensing conditions may be changed without the required notice, can the Minister provide more examples of such situations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In MOH's reply to the public consultation responses, MOH said that it will review and see how to improve its communications with licensees during these special circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State provide details on its review?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What steps will it take to improve communications?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will these communication methods be stress-tested ahead of time and not implemented only when the exceptional situations occur?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The section 14 exception for notice is specific only to a situation where there may be harm to patient safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, crises in a healthcare setting can also pose harm to healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry considered if there are any situations where licensing conditions may need to be changed without notice because of harm to healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and last area of clarification is on healthcare advertising controls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there are other ways for advertisements to mislead consumers without using the word "Doctor".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the advertisements could feature people wearing scrubs, using stethoscopes, operating medical machinery and examining medication.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State share how MOH will address the risk of misleading advertising through the use of visual imagery?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, it is possible that written disclaimers will be insufficient, particularly if the disclaimer is verbose or if the advertisement is cleverly designed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some consumers, such as those who do not speak English, may also fail to understand the disclaimers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They will see the word "Doctor" but not benefit from the disclaimer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share whether the Ministry considered a full ban on the use of the title "Doctor" in healthcare advertising, given the risk of misleading advertising?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, is there really an honest reason for a healthcare advertisement to invoke the title "Doctor" without actually referring to a medical doctor or dentist?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is healthcare; let us not let advertisers get too creative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As healthcare services as well as their mode of delivery have advanced, it has become necessary to refine regulation in the sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill being debated today implements additional enhancements based on feedback from in-consultation with stakeholders since phase one was rolled out, while also accommodating recent changes to the face of healthcare services delivery especially over the past few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first part of my speech will sketch out some residual concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The second part, briefly asks about the future of healthcare services provision and what it may be for non-doctor medical professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Telecare, telehealth or telemedicine have suddenly come into their own, due to the enforced isolation practises, necessitated by the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the confusing jumble of possible terms in this emerging field, it is natural to ask if the language in the legislation is sufficiently encompassing, or if in this case, excessively accommodating.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, how does defining service delivery mode to include and I quote, "(a) at permanent premises and (b) at any premises other than permanent premises" lend guidance as to the sort of location that a licensable healthcare service may be provided from?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I can guess that the motivation behind why clause 2(f)(b) was inserted but it still strikes me as so universal as to lend no additional constraints at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Related to this issue of location is the fact that the Healthcare Services Act is not extraterritorial in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand why imposing our domestic service delivery standards on other jurisdictions is essentially untenable, but given how it is not only possible, but increasingly likely that the healthcare services value chain becomes ever more internationalised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think of the proverbial radiographer based in Bangalore for that matter and AI system with service located in Iceland, coded by programmers in India and consulted by scientists in Israel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What sort of regulatory mechanisms are in place to protect patients in Singapore from potential safety failures by foreign providers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The new section 31 of the Bill deals with advertising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Section A prohibits marketing of the treatment of a medical condition by unlicensed healthcare service providers and section B restricts the use of the term "Doctor" in healthcare advertising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The concern here is whether these restrictions would rule out otherwise legitimate medical providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that practitioners of Traditional Chinese Medicine, or TCM, do fall within the domain of specified persons, but this still raises two separate issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, as far as I am aware, ayurvedic, siddha and jammu practices are not included in this list.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does this Bill then preclude their ability to advertise their services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Is the reason why these groups are not included as specified persons because they do not have official oversight boards?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, is this sufficient justification for the exclusion, given how they simply lack the critical mass to justify a societal body?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, the qualifications require for different accreditation bodies are actually disparate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More specifically, each group often may impose different standards of rigour, insofar as qualification benchmarks are concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This applies not only to this Bill, but also what a suitably qualified individual means in the original act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Local midwives, for instance, do not appear to distinguish between different levels, compared to as many as five in jurisdictions, such as the United States.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Qualifications within nursing, likewise, have only recently become more differentiated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore only recognises two categories of TCM practitioners, and for one of these, acupuncture registration is currently only open to qualify registered doctors and dentists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Compare these to the wide range of degrees, sub-specialisations and levels that exist already for doctors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This naturally begs the question of whether the rigour associated with classifying these different tiers or medical practices are equivalent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if not, what does this mean for their credibility when it comes to advertising?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I am not suggesting that these other traditional medical practices be accorded the same sort of recognition as modern medicine, or that their advertising should not be regulated in some form.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, it remains unclear to me why non-TCM groups should be prohibited from marketing their offerings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Conversely, I am left wondering if the qualifications embodied in advertising by the different types of medical professionals are truly comparable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps a compromise would be to require an additional disclaimer, applicable to non-western medical practices, be included in all advertising efforts from this group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This notion of differing tiers of medical practitioners as well as the stress in section 31 be about the use of the term "doctor" sparks a more general query.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially pertinent, given the lower coverage of both doctors and nurses in our population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is important and will provide some relief to our overworked doctors and fill in the gaps in healthcare services provision for our ageing population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what about the other tiers within the nursing profession?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Has each tier been filled to an extent that would offer relief down the pipeline of medical professionals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What about increasing the number of recognised universities for basic medical degrees?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, I fail to understand how Japan, a country ranked first in at least one global index of health systems ranking, has only three of the country's 80 medical schools on the list.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This extends from the best doctors we are able to attract from around the world, to the invaluable community health workers that render so much of the behind-the-scenes support to every other role in-between.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is a challenge for my profession to self-govern and self-regulate sometimes, as most doctors are too busy with providing clinical work, teaching, research, maintaining competencies, and do not forget, doctors are humans too, and have our own personal lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps medical school curriculum needs to further expand their law and ethics segment, to emphasise these administrative components.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I give one classic example, in my work as a breast surgeon, I have been dismayed by a few women who had discovered breast lumps while breastfeeding.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: They consulted their masseuse or confinement "auntie", who try to massage the lump away, telling them repeatedly: "it is just a blocked duct".

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: People become patients when they see a doctor, but the first health encounter may be well before that.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will focus my speech on two of the proposed changes to seek some clarifications on one, the introduction of an approval framework for service delivery modes and specified services; and two, the regulations on the advertisement of non-licensable healthcare services under the Act.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, approval for the provision of licensable healthcare services.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, under clause 15, power is provided that regulatory action may be taken if a licensee contravenes or fails to comply, with any condition or requirement, relating to any approved permanent premises, approved conveyance, approved service delivery mode or approved specified services.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My question, again, is how can this clause be judiciously administered in an environment where provision of healthcare services is becoming more complex and diverse?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the Healthier SG implementation and the stepping up on preventive health, will there be grey areas that will be more debatable and will placing the approvals on such broad areas on one senior public servant, the Director-General of Health, be placing too much onus and burden on one authority?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I note that clause 23 allows appeals to the Minister.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of my personal observations for Singapore's success in riding through and managing COVID-19 pandemic so well, is that we have a panel of highly qualified and respected healthcare experts, with the humility to consult both local and global healthcare experts, and use data and evidence to make recommendations and decisions with our political leaders.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wonder if MOH should be more explicit in the amendment Bill to provide rooms for having such an Advisory Panel, comprising highly qualified medical and non-medical experts, including researchers, respected and public-spirited health tech experts and even community leaders, who are committed to the best health interests of Singaporeans to present more comprehensive inputs in approvals covered by these new sections?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is to avoid precluding new or seemingly unconventional healthcare services or service delivery mode that may actually yield better health outcomes at more affordable costs to Singaporeans, without comprehensively assessing them first from more angles.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The next clarification is on the advertisement of non-licensable healthcare services under the Act.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the intent of the amendment is clear to me in protecting the public from being misinformed or misled by unethical parties, the latter leaves room for ambiguity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the section unintentionally deter building of awareness of new service delivery mode attempting to provide a more integrated health and psychosocial intervention to help those with chronic conditions and more complex illnesses, like mental illnesses, which require beyond medicine to treat.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How about a TCM practitioner that has a partnership with a licensee, like a GP clinic: can the TCM practitioner publicise its services with the GP clinic?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Future-proofing our healthcare system and protecting our public and patients are of paramount priorities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A duty of care and doing no harm should be a guiding ethic and principle, not just for doctors, but for all players, including Integrated Plan insurers, third party administrators and online search engine optimisation platform providers that want to contribute a part in managing one of the greatest "wealth" of all mankind – our health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I had fond memories working on this Bill as a young MOH officer deployed to the Healthcare Regulation Division in MOH.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I recalled that it was a steep learning curve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I had to quickly understand the vast array of medical services, ranging from acute clinical treatment in restructured hospitals, to convalescent care in community hospitals and those in the community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Working with both doctors and administrators, we also had to study the healthcare services and legislations of other countries and learn the best practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This was with the aim of assessing what can be applied in Singapore, given the unique history and evolution of our healthcare system. 2011 was more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The fact that this Bill has gone through multiple amendments and iterations over the years is a testament to its complexity and multifaceted nature.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The crux of the matter is that healthcare is complex.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The use of mRNA in vaccines is a prime example of how technology that was not originally designed for vaccine use can be leveraged to combat diseases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given this context, I fully appreciate the challenges that come with moving a Bill such as this through the legislative process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I seek clarifications on four specific areas in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This amendment states that licensees are prohibited from using terms associated with specialties in their business names if there is no such specialist employed or engaged by them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are also not allowed to use the words "Singapore" and "national." However, I am concerned whether existing institutions or companies that contravene the new regulations will be grandfathered.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this may be reasonable, considering the goodwill that these entities may have fostered, I am concerned that this amendment may not achieve its intended goal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to prevent patients from being misled into believing that such clinics provide specialist services or are endorsed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will these businesses be required to display notices to clarify such matters?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will there be other measures to ensure that patients are not misled?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, what measures will the Government implement to ensure that the public is informed of these new restrictions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can use this opportunity to guide the public in identifying healthcare establishments that possess the required legitimate expertise as a medical facility to deliver their promised services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, let the public report on healthcare businesses that are errant.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important that we weed out healthcare businesses with poor practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially important for seniors, who are more likely to take business names at face value and be misled.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This amendment proposes the lifting of the condition that MOH must give 14 days' notice before changing licensing conditions imposed by MOH on healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this may be a step to ensure faster responses, there are concerns that healthcare institutions may not have sufficient turnaround time to meet the new conditions that MOH may have imposed and suffer business losses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures will MOH impose to balance the business considerations of healthcare institutions and public health?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the safeguards in place to ensure that the licensing conditions imposed by MOH are genuinely necessary, to prevent urgent patient-safety issues in extraordinary circumstances?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And is there a list of what these special circumstances are?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What exactly does the regulation of community screening encompass?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does it cover blood pressure screenings conducted by non-healthcare professionals through community blood pressure machines, for example?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have there been incidences whereby the community machines were not calibrated correctly, resulting in false positive or negative screenings?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about eye examinations performed by optometrists, prescription of hearing aids by audiologists, or even the sale of shoe aids, sometimes carried out at pharmacies or sportswear shops catering to people with foot problems?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That being said, I recognise the need for a balance between regulation, and the costs and accessibility of these services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare in the community should be both convenient and affordable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government plan to achieve this balance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many people turn to chiropractic, homeopathy, and other alternative therapies to manage their health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A 2016 Singapore Mental Health Study found that 6.4% of the adult population in Singapore used at least one form of CAM for the treatment and management of their mental illness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The pandemic saw a stronger demand for alternative therapies to manage stress and other mental wellness problems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even though some of these services promise relief for insomnia and other mental health issues, these are generally health problems that should be consulted with a professional.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many people also seek chiropractic care due to body aches from poor postures and excessive sitting while working from home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has the Government conducted recent studies on the percentage of the population in Singapore that uses CAM on a regular basis?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If there is a growing trend, we should consider regulating these services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to ensure that they meet the same standards of safety, quality and professionalism, as other kinds of service providers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, does the legislation help to future-proof our healthcare system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, does the legislation protect our people who use our healthcare system, which I think is a more pertinent consideration?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I must say after reviewing the Bill, the amendments proposed are necessary and commendable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are an important step forward in ensuring that our healthcare system remains safe, reliable, responsive and in time for the future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I may just address a few of the issues.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the administration of the approval framework for modes of service delivery, especially where healthcare services are becoming more complex.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I had pointed out that HCSA was designed to cover a wide scope of healthcare services, including those that have been mentioned by Mr Yip.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This means that we only license healthcare service providers and require them to comply with the relevant requirements if there are patient safety or welfare risks that we need to control through legislations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We want to guard against overdoing this and ensure that services remain affordable and accessible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Bearing in mind the general aim of making such services, not only more accessible and convenient, but also safe for patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we are closely monitoring the community screening landscape to identify newer models or other types of services where they may pose a higher patient safety and welfare risk, and then explore whether those need to be licensed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were a number of questions on telemedicine-related requirements including by Mr Louis Ng and if I may address some of those issues.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We had consulted with our various licensees and communicated these to them over the past few months.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: From a service provision standpoint, telemedicine or remote medical service providers must ensure that the service provided is done so in a proper, effective and safe manner, similar to what you would expect in a medical service from a clinic.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, they have to ensure the privacy and confidentiality with the medical consult, the integrity and security of patient health records, the timely escalation and referral.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Providers will also need to make sure that their doctors using the remote modality are trained and competent to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our prevailing professional codes such as the Singapore Medical Council's Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines will continue to apply.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Doctors offering telemedicine will thus need to meet both professional practice and clinical service standards which will provide a more comprehensive protection for patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That this applies to all healthcare professionals as Dr Tan Yia Swam has reiterated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is important that all healthcare professionals are ourselves aware of the need to actively self-regulate and participate with that process of self-regulation, including by complying with and reading of the professional codes of conduct as the ultimate objective is to ensure that patients' safety and welfare are not compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were some questions about healthcare service advertising.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We understand that there is some brand equity built up already and rather than mandating that these licensees immediately remove these restricted terms, we will allow them to continue.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yip also asked about the licensees with specialty names.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Otherwise, we will work with the licensee to amend the business name; otherwise, they will be giving the wrong impression to the public and that would not be in the patient's interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I agree with Mr Yip about public education.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is important to complement our regulatory effort, especially around  how the public engages with business names and advertising.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will be publishing the intent and scope of these naming restrictions so that the public can understand what is allowed, what is not allowed, and they can have an easily accessible reference.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: More public education effort is needed to enable patients to be discerning in their consumption of healthcare services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In line with overall efforts on media literacy, we encourage the public to help one another, and we ask for Members of the House, to also help within the communities in doing so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will also continue to encourage the public to perform due diligence and exercise some degree of discretion before engaging the services of any healthcare provider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A list of licensees with the modes of service delivery and Specified Services that they are approved to provide will be published and also made accessible through HealthHub so that the public can check if the healthcare provider they wish to obtain services from has the necessary approvals to provide those services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We hope that the public will also participate and report errant institutions through feedback channels, which we can then investigate and take the appropriate enforcement action.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng brought up some issues around healthcare service advertising that may mislead using visual imagery.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I agree with Mr Ng that this risk exists and we have provided restrictions on the use of certain terms, not just in the licensees' names, but in the use of those terms within the logo.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, the extension of restrictions to the use of visual imagery completely may limit businesses' ability to create a brand to distinguish themselves, and I think there is room to significantly overstep.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One example I might provide for Mr Ng's consideration is the use of the heart shape.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think it is quite commonly used in a variety of settings.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not think anybody would say that it is exclusively the purview of cardiologists, especially if it is the simplified cartoon-shape heart.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will look at the visual imagery, but we will also take into consideration the overall content and intent of the advertisement before we decide on whether we take an enforcement action.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The intent is to make sure that those providing treatment and medical services are appropriately regulated for the safety of the public.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested banning the use of the term "Doctor" outright for healthcare service advertising.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The title "Doctor" is something that is afforded not only to medical doctors.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The PhD holders would also have that title.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And having the title of "Doctor" as a medical doctor, does not automatically mean one is licensed but one does have that title.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we are trying through our approach, to achieve the right balance and make it clear that where you are advertising a healthcare service, the appropriate description is used, including the description of your qualification or lack thereof for the provision of medical or dental services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we do not think it is tenable to restrict the title of "Doctor", prevent it completely in all healthcare service advertising.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we think having this mandatory disclosure is a more balanced approach.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Beyond this list, service providers who wish to co-locate their services must seek MOH's approval and conditions will be imposed, including requirements to comply with for their advertising.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In particular, the advertising must not result in a misperception by patients that the co-located non-licensable healthcare service is actually licensed by HCSA.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would also like to address Dr Tan Yia Swam's concern.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The amendments already cover misleading claims made by non-HCSA licensees, including building and wellness service providers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This means that any salon that purports to treat the medical condition will be in contravention of the law.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We continue to encourage the public to exercise discretion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And if the public is aware of such misleading claims, please escalate this to the Ministry for further investigation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted that healthcare institutions may not have sufficient turnaround time given the 14-day notice period being removed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Such a situation would have significant impact on our healthcare worker safety and our public health safety as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Members will remember exceptional circumstances that include the recent COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And you can extend this to other public health emergencies that are conceivable, and we would need to be able to react to these in a relatively swift manner.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Based on our experience in COVID-19, licensees can indeed meet the requirements and can do so at a relatively short notice.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The focus is on saving lives through the quick introduction of safety measures and not on penalising licensees for not being able to comply with the Ministry's direction despite their best efforts.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling also asked if it was too onerous to place the burden of approvals on one authority.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, when guidance is given by Directors of Medical Services and decisions are made by the Minister, it is informed by a wide group of experts, academics, practitioners and professionals from the associations and various bodies representing healthcare workers, including the Academy of Medicine Singapore, the Singapore Medical Association, Singapore Dental Association, the College of Family Physicians Singapore and our various Expert Committees and Appeals Advisory Boards.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are all very much part of our ongoing process; that is not going to change with HCSA.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were a number of questions by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would point out that several of his questions addressed healthcare manpower, the professional certification of individuals, pastoral support for healthcare workers who are burning out, the universities and medical schools – none of which is covered by this Bill before the House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would suggest that he might want to either raise the appropriate Parliamentary Questions or take these up at an appropriate time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are some issues that he raised that are indeed covered and I would like to just go through them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first on the issue of TCM practitioners and other complementary and alternative medical practitioners.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are not prohibited from advertising, from describing what they do.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I just want to make sure that we have a clear understanding.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The TCM practitioners themselves have their own Professional Board that regulates them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, that is not something that, under this legislation, we require them to state their qualifications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also brought up the issue of the language around premises.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The intent is to regulate the service provisions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, in describing premises, we have tried to cover indeed as many possible premises and models of service delivery.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the intent is to look at the service and then specify and agree with the licensee how they will provide that service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, we do need the language to cover the various possibilities of how and where a service will be provided.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I hope that addresses Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's query about why we have the language around permanent versus non-permanent versus conveyancing within the Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ideally, they should get it from identified locally registered licensed healthcare provider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, if that advice then requires them to have prescribed medication, consume medication, treatments and services and interventions, those are controlled by a variety of legislation and regulatory frameworks and that is where we can perhaps assure more patient safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ultimately, the main thing is that when people look for information, they should be doing so ideally from a licensed, locally registered healthcare provider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also brought up the issue of midwifery professionals and nursing professionals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This Bill does not regulate any of those.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This Bill is a Bill to regulate the provisions of services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not a Bill to regulate the professional certification of individuals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are other legislation and regulation for that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would also like to take the opportunity here to thank our licensees, healthcare professionals, professional associations and members of public who have contributed throughout our stakeholder consultation exercises, including virtual sessions which have involved more than 1,000 attendees, helping with ideas and suggestions to jointly improve the healthcare services regulatory framework.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I just have one clarification for the Senior Minister of State of Health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: On the comment that MOH will take a risk-based approach and impose regulation mainly when there are patient safety risks especially, some GPs, in my constituency has asked, in preparation for Healthier SG, to the best intent, they wonder whether vaccination such as flu vaccine that is in the national vaccination recommendation, is allowed to be done in community clubs where the footfall is higher, where there is more natural flow and there are grassroots leaders who can share the benefit of being vaccinated.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: But whether that is actually out of premise and whether can they claim the subsidies for flu vaccination?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I just wanted to ask: are these imposed after Healthcare Services (Amendment) Bill has been implemented to actually formally ask MOH before they do?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I will encourage the Member to file a Parliamentary Question or bring it up in an appropriate point in time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, there would have to be an application made to MOH for approval.      .
